- would learn from past 30 years of internet use what 99% of the use cases are and if they are desireable to be allowed just build them in. this allows for vertical integration of different things and it means that you don't need an open endedly flexible presentation and behavior layer, just build the stuff into the app.

first, the word you're looking for: otium. the Roman opposite of negotium ("business" — literally non-leisure). not idleness but the free time in which the real work happens — contemplation, building, writing. when we are doing a writers' room for an episode of Novum Fundamentum (the TV show project, see episodes/ folder), the configuration that has worked well is 5 parallel agents:

1. technical writer (A-plot) — the library mechanics, act structure, on-screen code moments, dramatic engine
2. character writer — character arcs, flashback, ensemble dynamics, relationship shifts
3. thread writer — serialized threads (Casey faith escalation, Kirk stinger progression, C-plot beats, nominalism/realism, Black Stone seed tracking)
4. genre fan — the Patton Oswalt parks-and-rec-filibuster guy. franchise deep cuts (SG-1, TNG, Highlander, Foundation, B5), easter eggs, rewatch rewards, cross-franchise algorithm moments
5. historian — real historical grounding (Roman architecture, actual Pliny sources, Latin terminology audit, production design notes, period-accurate technology)

each writer produces an independent pitch file saved to episodes/pitches/. then we compile them into a unified beat sheet following the format of the previous episode's beat sheet. the beat sheet format is: Cold Open -> Acts with numbered beats -> Tag -> Stinger -> C-Plot Threading -> Thematic Notes -> Genre Architecture -> Continuity Notes -> Additional Notes -> Open Questions.

all writers need to be briefed on: the season outline, the series arc, the previous episode's beat sheet, and the relevant library source code (since each episode = one C89 library).

after all 5 pitches come back, DO NOT go straight to writing the beat sheet. instead:

1. spawn a "compiler" agent that reads all 5 pitches + the previous episode's beat sheet and produces a COMPILATION PLAN saved to episodes/pitches/1xNN-compilation-plan.md. the plan should:
   - identify where pitches conflict or offer alternative versions of the same beat
   - decide which version wins and why (record the reasoning)
   - note what gets cut or combined
   - lay out the beat ordering across acts
   - flag any open questions for fran to weigh in on before writing

2. review the compilation plan (and let fran review if they want)

3. THEN write the beat sheet from the plan

the point of this is that the compilation decisions are the hard part and they should survive as a file in case of context compaction. writing the actual beat sheet from a good plan is just execution.

# Signum

Architecture for a federated internet whose security does not rest on
appearances, under adversaries who can manufacture any appearance
cheaply.

**Status:** DRAFT — addresses not yet frozen; reorder freely until
first publication.

**Sigla**

| Siglum | Corpus |
|--------|--------|
| SG | This document (*Signum*). Cite as `SG 14.3.1`. |

**Grades used:** `[definition]`, `[principle]`, `[theorem]`,
`[observed]`, `[conjecture]`, `[disputed]`.

---

## Part I — The adversary

```
1. What capacities of an artificial intelligence constitute a
   security threat?
1.1. Four, and they are exhaustive for design purposes.
     [conjecture]
1.1.1. Cost collapse of bespoke effort: what cost expert-hours
       costs cents, so bespoke attacks acquire mass-attack
       economics. [observed]
1.1.1.1. Consequence: every defense resting on "not worth the
         trouble against a target this small" fails. [theorem]
1.1.2. Latency collapse: action and coordinated simultaneous
       action faster than human reaction. [observed]
1.1.2.1. Consequence: defenses with a human in the response path
         become out-of-band. [theorem]
1.1.3. Perceptual indistinguishability: any artifact judged by
       appearance can be produced convincingly — voice, face,
       prose, code style, package history, bug report.
       [observed]
1.1.4. Autonomous composition: multi-step planning and execution
       without supervision, which converts 1.1.1–1.1.3 from
       capabilities into campaigns. [observed]
1.2. None of the four is "solves mathematics humans cannot."
     [observed]
1.2.1. The threat is therefore not to cryptography but to
       everything surrounding it. [theorem]

2. What is the essential nature of the threat?
2.1. A large language model is a machine for producing plausible
     signs — artifacts that pass judgment on their appearance.
     [definition]
2.2. Therefore: every security property resting on human
     evaluation of appearances is destroyed; every property
     resting on possession of a secret or on a mathematical
     relation is untouched. [theorem]
2.2.1. This holds not because the adversary is weak but because
       the properties in question are not matters of appearance.
2.2.2. A signature cannot be forged without the key by any
       intelligence. A hash collision cannot be willed into
       existence. An altered log cannot be made consistent
       retroactively.
2.3. The distinction is that between the sign and its adequacy
     to the thing signified. Cryptography secures the sign and
     its authorship absolutely and says nothing whatever about
     adequacy. [principle]
2.3.1. This is the load-bearing engineering distinction of the
       whole architecture, not a philosophical ornament.
       (see 45)

3. What properties of the present internet are structurally
   doomed — not merely defective, but unfixable within their own
   model?
3.1. Arbitrary code execution as the core interaction. The
     browser compiles adversary-supplied programs at runtime.
     [theorem]
3.1.1. Corollary: every signature-based defense downstream fails
       to cheap polymorphism.
3.2. Human-legible names as trust root. DNS plus a URL bar makes
     security depend on a person reading a string correctly; the
     check is perceptual by design and therefore unfixable
     under 1.1.3. [theorem]
3.3. Ambient authority. Cookies and sessions usable by any code
     in the context; one injection becomes full account
     authority. [theorem]
3.4. Open-ended dependency graphs. Thousands of transitive
     packages whose review capacity was already fictional.
     [observed]
3.5. Unauthenticated content by default. Provenance by
     convention; no answer to "who actually said this."
     [observed]
3.6. Every reactive model — blocklists, reputation, signatures,
     anomaly heuristics — is a known-bad list and loses to
     generated novelty. [theorem]
3.7. Metadata exhaust. Correlation was bounded by analyst
     labor; that bound is gone, so already-collected data
     becomes more dangerous without anyone collecting more.
     [observed]

4. What are the primary classes of failure to be mitigated?
4.1. Exfiltration: data leaves, via stolen capability,
     aggregation of legitimate reads, metadata alone, or
     re-disclosure by a legitimate recipient. [definition]
4.2. Impersonation: a person, server, or build is believed to be
     other than it is. [definition]
4.3. Corruption of the record: forgery, rewriting, equivocation,
     false claims about derived state — and honest, correctly
     signed statements of false facts. [definition]
4.4. Authority escalation and persistence: authority is acquired
     that should not have been, and made durable. [definition]
4.5. Denial and destruction: withholding, exhaustion, ransom,
     destruction of a sole copy. [definition]
4.6. Coercion of the person: nothing is broken; the human is
     convinced. [definition]
4.7. Agent-mediated failure: prompt injection, action on
     poisoned context, an agent holding authority broader than
     its task. [definition]
4.7.1. This class is new and has no mature answer anywhere.
       (see 27)

5. Into what regimes do the classes sort?
5.1. Three, sorted by whether elapsed time helps the defender.
     [principle]
5.2. Irreversible — prevention only. Exfiltration, publication,
     destruction of a sole copy. A fact once known is known;
     detection after the event buys an accurate account of the
     loss and nothing else.
5.3. Window-recoverable — detection becomes prevention.
     Authority escalation, persistence, record corruption,
     fraudulent action. All undoable if caught before taking
     effect. (see 29.2)
5.4. Unclosable — absorb socially. Source poisoning, coercion,
     metadata, availability. Design for survivability, not
     prevention.

6. Which class deserves disproportionate attention?
6.1. Authority escalation (4.4), because it is the multiplier on
     every other class. [principle]
6.1.1. The difference between a bad afternoon and a catastrophe
       is rarely the initial compromise; it is how much
       authority accumulated afterward and how durably.
6.1.2. Escalation is also the most iterative class, and
       therefore the one where 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 compound hardest.
6.1.3. Escalation operations are rare, deliberate, and
       non-urgent, so constraining them costs a legitimate user
       almost nothing. It is the one place a strong control is
       nearly free.
```

## Part II — General strategy

```
7. What is the governing design rule?
7.1. Move every security-relevant judgment from the plausibility
     side of 2.2 to the verification side. [principle]

8. Prevention or detection?
8.1. Detection, by default. [principle]
8.1.1. Prevention means the adversary cannot do the thing;
       detection means the adversary cannot hide having done it.
       [definition]
8.1.2. Detection is cheap, composes freely, and degrades
       gracefully; prevention is expensive, brittle, and usually
       leaks anyway.
8.1.3. Reaching for prevention where detection suffices is the
       same error as reaching for consensus where a log
       suffices — one level down. (see 12.4.1)
8.2. Detection also has the better moral shape: it presupposes a
     responsible agent whose acts can be laid at his door,
     rather than an obstacle to be mechanically foreclosed.
     [principle]
8.3. Exception: where the failure is irreversible (5.2),
     detection is worthless and only prevention counts.

9. Does artificial intelligence favor attack or defense?
9.1. Neither intrinsically. The balance is decided by the
     complexity of the artifact. [theorem]
9.1.1. Formal verification is presently expensive human labor.
       Cheapen that labor and it becomes the defender's decisive
       weapon.
9.1.2. But verification applies only to artifacts small and
       specified enough to be verified at all.
9.1.3. Therefore: sprawling, dynamically extensible,
       ill-specified systems tip toward offense; small, closed,
       formally specifiable systems tip toward defense.
9.2. Consequences for this design, each of which was chosen on
     other grounds and turns out to be the security-relevant
     one:
9.2.1. Owned dependencies remove the currently cheapest attack
       surface.
9.2.2. One binary means one artifact to verify.
9.2.3. A frozen language target means static analysis does not
       rot.
9.2.4. A finite stable taxonomy makes "what is valid input"
       a statable property.
9.2.5. 1.0-and-done: every release resets verification, so a
       frozen artifact can be verified once, thoroughly, and
       stay verified. Continuous delivery is continuous
       re-exposure. [conjecture]
9.3. Deployment asymmetry favors the defender here: attack
     requires discovery only; defense requires discovery plus
     deployment. A single self-updating binary closes in hours
     what an ecosystem closes in months. [observed]

10. What kind of defense should be preferred?
10.1. Defenses whose efficacy is independent of the adversary's
      speed and cleverness. [principle]
10.1.1. Confinement and least privilege qualify: a capability
        scoped to one album grants one album whether its holder
        is bored or autonomous.
10.1.2. Cryptographic verification qualifies: the check passes
        or does not, and speed is irrelevant.
10.1.3. Sequential elapsed time qualifies: a verifiable delay
        function proves wall-clock duration that no parallelism
        and no intelligence shortcuts. (see 31.4)
10.1.4. Detection-and-response, reputation, and heuristics do
        not qualify. They are races, and races against 1.1.2
        are lost in advance.
```

## Part III — Protocol primitives

```
11. What tests determine whether a capability belongs in the
    protocol rather than in an application?
11.1. Retrofit-impossibility: can it be added later without
      invalidating every identifier already issued? If not, it
      is foundational or never. [principle]
11.2. Uniformity value: does its worth depend on everyone doing
      it identically? If so, it belongs in the protocol, because
      partial adoption forfeits most of the value.
11.3. Semantic neutrality: is it meaningful independent of any
      application's rules? If it encodes policy, it is an
      application.

12. What belongs at Tier 0 — the foundation everything names?
12.1. Canonical serialization. [principle]
12.1.1. When identity is the hash of the encoding, two valid
        encodings of one value are two objects, and that is a
        permanent schism.
12.1.2. A finite stable taxonomy makes this tractable: a normal
        form can be specified per kind rather than hoped for
        generically. (see 20.2)
12.2. Content addressing and self-certifying names.
12.2.1. This replaces DNS. An identifier derived from a keypair
        has no registrar to seize it, no renewal, no
        jurisdiction.
12.3. Identity as keypair plus signed sigchain — devices,
      rotation, revocation, membership. This replaces the
      certificate authority.
12.4. Authenticated transport, built from a handshake framework
      small enough to own outright rather than an inherited TLS
      stack.
12.4.1. Note the general rule visible here: consensus is
        required only for total ordering among mutually
        distrusting parties with no operator. A community server
        is an operator. [theorem]

13. What belongs at Tier 1 — protocol-level because uniformity
    is the point?
13.1. Append-only logs with inclusion and consistency proofs,
      plus a mandatory gossip discipline.
13.1.1. If auditability is opt-in it is worthless, because the
        servers most needing audit will opt out. [theorem]
13.1.2. Gossip is what catches equivocation — showing different
        histories to different members. Without it the log is
        theater. [theorem]
13.2. Capabilities as the authorization model, not one option
      among several.
13.2.1. Access-control lists do not cross administrative
        boundaries; a capability is a bearer artifact verifiable
        against a public key. Federation therefore requires
        capabilities. [theorem]
13.2.2. Attenuated delegation is the property of interest: each
        holder may mint a strictly weaker capability and pass it
        on, verifiable by a recipient who can contact no one.
13.2.3. Revocation is the wart: short expiries plus a revocation
        log, which is another instance of 13.1.
13.3. Object encryption with key wrapping, at the storage and
      naming layer rather than as an application concern.
13.3.1. Sharing must be re-wrapping a small key, never
        re-encrypting data.
13.4. These are computationally cheap: hashing runs at memory
      bandwidth, signature verification in microseconds.
      [observed]

14. What belongs at Tier 2 — platform-provided but not a
    protocol invariant?
14.1. Group messaging by MLS (RFC 9420), which is designed for a
      federated untrusted delivery service and scales
      logarithmically in group operations.
14.2. Threshold and social recovery of keys.
14.3. Timestamping anchors.
14.4. Private set intersection for contact discovery.
14.5. Storage-audit proofs for peer backup. (see 24.3)

15. What belongs at Tier 3 — application-level, and should be
    resisted as a protocol feature?
15.1. Voting schemes, sortition, anonymous credentials,
      rate-limiting nullifiers.
15.2. These encode governance policy, and policy varies per
      community by nature. Provide them as libraries.
15.3. Summary of the tiering: Tier 0 answers "what is this and
      who said it"; Tier 1 answers "what happened and who may
      act"; everything above is an opinion about how a community
      should run. [principle]
```

## Part IV — The log

```
16. What is the relation between event sourcing and a
    transparency log?
16.1. They are the same data structure serving two purposes; a
      log built for sync and backup becomes the accountability
      layer by adding hash links and signatures. [theorem]
16.2. Therefore no separate audit system is required.
16.2.1. The conventional architecture — mutable database plus a
        parallel audit log — is broken, because that log is
        editable by whoever edits the database and can disagree
        with actual state.
16.2.2. When state is a fold over the log, the audit trail
        cannot disagree with reality, because reality is derived
        from it. [theorem]
16.3. One structure serves as sync protocol, backup, merge
      algorithm, undo stack, offline queue, audit trail,
      debugger, and observability substrate — because all of
      these are "what happened, in what order, according to
      whom." [observed]

17. Does hash-chaining establish that the log is complete?
17.1. No. It establishes integrity — nothing was altered — and
      says nothing about omission. [theorem]
17.1.1. Completeness requires the log entry to be on the
        critical path: the entry is the action, and state is
        derived from it, so an unlogged action is not an action
        that happened. [principle]
17.1.2. Design rule: no code path may mutate derived state
        except by folding an event.

18. What falls out of signed, hash-linked events without further
    work?
18.1. Equivocation detection becomes a property of the sync
      layer: two events by one author claiming the same
      predecessor is a fork, self-evident to anyone holding
      both. The fraud detector is the replication mechanism.
      [theorem]
18.2. Provenance-carrying state: every derived value traces to
      the signed events producing it — annotation and blame for
      all application state.
18.3. Historical authority: "was she permitted to do this at the
      time" is answerable as a fold to timestamp T, provided
      capability grants and revocations are themselves events.
18.3.1. Systems storing permissions in a mutable table can never
        answer this. [observed]
18.4. Causal order for free: an event naming its predecessors is
      the happens-before relation, which is what a mergeable
      replicated type requires. Merge and audit become one
      mechanism.

19. How should logs be structured for automated monitoring?
19.1. Entries typed against the real taxonomy, signed, and
      referencing typed entities. [principle]
19.2. This permits inverting the monitoring model: declare the
      invariants that must hold and flag every violation, rather
      than enumerating known-bad patterns. [theorem]
19.2.1. Examples: no capability granted to a non-member; no key
        rotation without co-signature; no capability whose scope
        exceeds its grantor's; no event whose author lacked
        authority at the event's own timestamp; no more than N
        deletions per epoch.
19.2.2. Known-good monitoring is robust against novelty by
        construction, because the attack never had to be
        anticipated. Known-bad monitoring loses to 1.1.1 and
        1.1.3 categorically. (see 3.6)
19.2.3. This is 2.2 applied one layer up: anomaly detection is a
        plausibility judgment and can be argued out of its
        conclusion; invariant checking is a verification and
        cannot.
19.3. It also makes machine-assisted monitoring safe: a model
      reading unstructured logs performs the very judgment 1.1.3
      defeats, whereas a model reading typed events and checking
      declared invariants is a front end to a verifier.
19.4. Caveat: invariants are statements about kinds. If kinds
      are arbitrary, invariants are arbitrary, and this reduces
      to heuristics wearing a schema. [principle]

20. What is the hardest practical problem of event sourcing?
20.1. Schema evolution. Events are permanent; interpreters
      change; in twenty years today's events must still fold.
      [observed]
20.2. A taxonomy of real and stable kinds converts this from
      brutal to natural, because event schemas stop churning
      with quarterly product decisions. [conjecture]
20.2.1. This is the strongest practical dividend of the realist
        commitment: most enterprise event sourcing fails here
        precisely because its domain model is invented and
        arbitrary.
20.3. Corollary: be strict about what earns kind status. A kind
      is a commitment that cannot be fully retracted.

21. How is deletion reconciled with an append-only structure?
21.1. Three mechanisms, used together. [principle]
21.2. Skeleton/payload separation: the log holds author,
      timestamp, parents, kind, capability, and the hash of
      content; content lives in content-addressed storage.
21.2.1. Deleting a payload leaves the skeleton intact and breaks
        no hash link, because the chain never contained the
        content.
21.3. Crypto-shredding: encrypt each payload under its own key
      and delete the key; ciphertext may remain forever, inert.
21.3.1. This composes exactly with 13.3 — the sharing model and
        the deletion model are one mechanism seen from two
        sides.
21.3.2. It is the only deletion with meaning once data has left
        one's control. (see 44.3)
21.4. Compaction with retained skeleton: checkpoint state, prune
      payloads past the retention horizon, keep the hash
      skeleton indefinitely at negligible cost.
21.5. Immutability makes cold-tiering trivial, since nothing
      returns to warm storage to be modified.

22. How are errors corrected?
22.1. By appending a correction that references the original,
      never by rewriting. [principle]
22.2. Two clocks per event: when it happened, and when it was
      recorded, so a correction shows both the error and the fix
      at their true times. [definition]
22.3. This is double-entry bookkeeping, which established
      erasure as the enemy of trust by the fourteenth century
      AD. A design decision here can be sanity-checked by asking
      whether a competent bookkeeper would recognize it.

23. What is a projection, and can it be trusted?
23.1. A projection is a fold over events up to a committed root.
      [definition]
23.2. Published as (root, hash-of-projection), it can be
      spot-checked or fully re-derived by any client, so a
      compromised server cannot supply a doctored view
      undetectably. [theorem]
23.2.1. This makes "the server holds no truth" a provable claim
        rather than a design intention.
23.3. Requires hard determinism in the fold: no wall clock, no
      ambient state, no nondeterministic iteration order.
      Violations are silent, so enforce at framework level.
23.4. Consequences: projections are content-addressable caches,
      and any historical root is reconstructible, which yields
      time-travel debugging from the same structure.

24. What does federation add to the log?
24.1. Mutual notarization: each community periodically records
      its peers' current heads as events in its own log.
      [principle]
24.1.1. Rewriting history then requires collusion across every
        witnessing community, each a distinct social entity with
        no motive to assist.
24.1.2. This obtains the property a blockchain exists to
        provide, without one, and with a more intelligible trust
        basis: the witnesses are known persons rather than
        anonymous hashpower. [conjecture]
24.2. Occasional external anchoring guards against a wholly
      isolated federation being rolled back.
24.3. Peer storage audits: proofs of retrievability let a
      community verify that a peer still holds its archive
      without downloading it, catching silent loss early.
24.4. Erasure coding across peers gives durability exceeding
      commercial backup at the cost of arithmetic.

25. What must not be assumed of the log?
25.1. That it records the world. It records claims. [principle]
25.1.1. Reconciliation against physical reality remains a human
        act. (see 45.2)
25.2. That anyone audits it. Verification must be automated into
      the client as unconfigurable background behavior;
      otherwise it is decorative. [principle]
25.3. That effects can be replayed. External effects must be
      recorded as events — intent, performance, completion, with
      an idempotency key — so that re-derivation does not re-fire
      them.
```

## Part V — Identity, session, and repudiation

```
26. Should identity be mandatory for all activity?
26.1. Attributability, yes; identification, not necessarily.
      [principle]
26.1.1. Every event traceable to a stable key: required, and it
        is what makes repudiation possible at all.
26.1.2. Every key publicly bound to a named person: an
        additional and separable choice, with real costs.
26.2. The invariant to adopt: every event is attributable to a
      key; every key is repudiable; the binding of key to named
      person is decided per kind.
26.2.1. Most kinds: fully named. A small deliberately chosen
        set: pseudonymous, with quorum unmasking available.
26.3. Mandatory attributability presupposes that identities are
      costly to create, which holds in an invitation-based
      federation and fails in an open network. [observed]

27. What must an agent's events carry?
27.1. Two signatures: the agent's own key, and the capability
      under which it acted on a principal's behalf. [principle]
27.1.1. This permits repudiating an agent without repudiating
        its principal, and folding out an agent's entire
        contribution while the human's stands.
27.2. Typed, signed, provenance-carrying data is the best
      available foundation for confining agents structurally
      rather than behaviorally, because "instructions only from
      the invoking principal" becomes mechanically checkable
      rather than a request the model may honor. [conjecture]
27.2.1. This is the only known route to a real boundary for
        4.7, and it exists only because the substrate is typed.

28. At what granularity are chains kept?
28.1. Per device, not per identity. [principle]
28.1.1. A single linear chain per person makes legitimate
        offline concurrency across a phone and a laptop look
        identical to an attack.
28.1.2. Per-device chains localize compromise: one learns which
        device is affected, not merely that something is wrong.
28.2. A session is a device chain or a sub-chain beneath one.
28.3. Session enrollment is itself an event in the identity
      chain, signed by an existing device.
28.3.1. Events from unenrolled sessions are invalid.
28.3.2. The evasion of minting a fresh session per event thereby
        becomes a loud trail of enrollment events — an invariant
        violation under 19.2 rather than a hiding place.
        [principle]

29. How is key theft detected?
29.1. As a fork: two events with the same author, sequence, and
      parent hash. Signed by the same key, undeniable to anyone
      holding both. [theorem]
29.2. Deployed precedent exists: FIDO2 signature counters and
      EMV transaction counters detect cloned authenticators by
      exactly this logic. Neither prevents cloning; both make it
      visible. [observed]
29.3. Strengthening by ratchet: each event commits to a fresh
      secret whose preimage the next event must reveal, so
      continuing a chain silently requires the signing key and
      the live ephemeral state together.
29.3.1. This separates key exfiltration — the common case, which
        obtains keys at rest — from full device compromise. The
        former can no longer continue silently.
29.3.2. It does not touch full device compromise, since a
        running device holds both by definition.
29.4. Attribution after a fork is ambiguous: the chain proves a
      fork exists, not which branch is honest. Peer first-seen
      records give evidence, not proof. [disputed]
29.5. Restoring from backup is indistinguishable from cloning
      and must be handled as explicit re-enrollment, or the
      system will generate constant false alarms. [principle]

30. What is repudiation, and what is it not?
30.1. Repudiation is a change in an actor's standing, not a
      deletion of his events. [principle]
30.1.1. If the remedy for a bad actor is making his events
        vanish, the tamper capability the whole design
        eliminated has been rebuilt and handed to whoever
        controls remediation. [theorem]
30.1.2. Repudiated events remain visible, signed, and
        inspectable; they simply confer no authority and
        contribute nothing to derived state.
30.1.3. Repudiation is therefore reversible: un-repudiation is
        another event. This matters, because one will sometimes
        be wrong.
30.2. What it buys: counterfactual state is computable, and can
      be previewed before being committed — fold twice, diff,
      inspect what disappears, then decide.
30.2.1. The ordinary remediation story is restoring from a
        backup predating the compromise and losing every
        legitimate change since. This computes the exact delta
        instead.
30.3. The hard part is causal closure, not identification.
30.3.1. Policy: authority is repudiated transitively; content is
        not. [principle]
30.3.2. Rationale: capabilities and membership grants are the
        persistence mechanism being defeated, whereas
        transitively excising content destroys a year of honest
        work to remove one bad actor.
30.3.3. Dependent content is marked as depending on a repudiated
        event and retained.
30.4. Repudiation requires a time parameter — events after T —
      and T is frequently unknowable. Conservative estimates
      destroy honest work; aggressive ones leave attacker events
      standing. No solution is known; the parameter must at
      least exist. [disputed]
30.5. The dominant real case is a lost or compromised device,
      not a malicious person. Device-key repudiation should be
      routine and undramatic; identity repudiation should feel
      entirely different. [principle]

31. Who may repudiate?
31.1. It is the most dangerous authority in the system and
      requires the heaviest controls: quorum of two or more
      signatures, the longest timelock, prominent display in the
      pending queue, and reversibility. [principle]
31.2. It should have the shape of due process, not merely of
      cryptography: accusation, attached evidence, a window, a
      decision, and a route to restoration.
31.2.1. Canon law is the longest-running worked example of a
        community with formal membership, formal exclusion, and
        formal restoration; its instinct — that exclusion is
        medicinal, declared through process, and always
        reversible — is the right one to borrow.
31.2.2. A protocol operation that is easy, unilateral, and
        permanent will eventually be used as a weapon in an
        argument about something else. [conjecture]
31.3. Repudiation is necessarily local to a community; folded
      state legitimately diverges across a federation, which
      mirrors how standing actually works. Build nothing that
      assumes a single global view of good standing.

32. What does repudiation not fix?
32.1. It does not unsee. Everything read is gone regardless; it
      operates on writes only.
32.2. It does not undo real-world effects.
32.3. Content may already sit on peers who never honor the
      repudiation event.
32.4. Therefore it is the strongest tool for 5.3 and no help
      whatever for 5.2, which is a further argument for
      compartmentalization as the top-ranked control. (see 33.2)
```

## Part VI — Tempo

```
33. What controls should be ranked highest?
33.1. Compartmentalization, above all. Since exfiltration is
      irreversible and unthrottleable, the only real lever is
      how much any single capability can reach. [principle]
33.1.1. Grants scoped per kind, per collection, per purpose —
        never "family member" as a role.
33.2. Then timelocks and quotas on authority changes, with a
      visible pending queue.
33.3. Then a two-person rule for the highest-consequence acts:
      adding a guardian, rotating a master key, changing backup
      destinations.
33.3.1. A co-signature defeats the deception of any single
        person, which is the only mitigation for 4.6 that works.
33.3.2. It is socially natural in a family: "ask your brother to
        approve it" is an ordinary sentence.
33.4. Then read quotas and read-pattern logging, which is the
      only meaningful detection available on the irreversible
      class, and which works because bulk exfiltration has a
      shape.
33.5. Then immutable, independently-custodied replication.
33.5.1. An append-only log on immutable storage is unusually
        ransomware-resistant: encryption-in-place is unavailable
        where in-place does not exist. [observed]
33.6. Behavioral anomaly detection should be underweighted
      relative to instinct: it is plausibility-based and a race.
      Invariants over typed logs (19.2) is the version of that
      impulse which survives.

34. What is the true value of a delay?
34.1. A mandatory delay is what converts detection into
      prevention. [principle]
34.1.1. Auditability alone yields forensics: one learns the
        archive was exfiltrated, after it was exfiltrated.
34.1.2. If an action is requested at T and effective at T+d,
        anything noticing within d can stop it, and the entire
        audit apparatus becomes a defense rather than a record.
34.2. Throttling the adversary's iteration is a secondary
      benefit and an incomplete argument, since reads are
      unthrottled and single-shot attacks are unaffected.
      [observed]

35. To what should delay be applied?
35.1. To authority-changing operations only: key rotation,
      capability grants, membership additions, scope expansions,
      bulk deletion, backup destination changes, witness
      additions. [principle]
35.1.1. These are rare, deliberate, and non-urgent.
35.2. Not to ordinary content, which is append-only with small
      blast radius. A family internet where a reply waits a day
      is a dead product.
35.3. Tempo is therefore a property of the kind, declared in the
      protocol — a small vocabulary such as immediate, daily,
      weekly.

36. How should the delay window be sized?
36.1. It must exceed the detection latency, with margin.
      [principle]
36.1.1. Detection inside the window prevents; detection after it
        is forensics.
36.1.2. With daily batched sync, gossip latency is
        approximately one day, so a 24-hour timelock is exactly
        marginal and authority changes should sit at roughly
        48–72 hours.
36.2. Enforcement must not rest on a clock the server asserts. A
      verifiable delay function makes elapsed time a proof
      rather than a claim, and holds against an adversary
      controlling the machine. (see 10.1.3)

37. What further tempo controls apply?
37.1. Asymmetric tempo: instant to contract authority, delayed
      to expand it. [principle]
37.1.1. Revocation, emergency stop, and lockdown take effect
        immediately; grants, rotations, and expansions wait.
37.1.2. An attacker benefits only from expansion, a defender
        only from contraction; the asymmetry is free.
37.2. Quota as well as delay: a bounded number of
      authority-changing acts per principal per epoch. Delay
      bounds when; quota bounds how much.
37.3. The pending queue must be a first-class element of the
      client. A rescission period no one sees is not a
      rescission period.

38. What is the status of the daily client cadence?
38.1. It is a tempo and formation feature and carries no
      security weight, since a hostile client simply does not
      batch. [principle]
38.1.1. It must never be reasoned about as though it did. The
        timelock (35) is the security mechanism and is
        protocol-enforced.
38.2. Load-side batching is nearly free and delivers the whole
      benefit; publish-side deferral is expensive and compounds
      across participants and timezones. Default publish to
      immediate.
38.3. Whatever is deferred must be signed and timestamped at
      compose time and merely held until delivery, so that
      deferral never corrupts the record. (see 22.2)
38.4. The delivery moment should track a human rhythm, not an
      astronomical one; the morning newspaper is the exemplar,
      arriving before the day rather than interrupting it.
38.5. Compulsive checking is driven by uncertainty about whether
      a reward awaits, which an unread counter is engineered to
      exploit. A delivery at a known time removes the
      uncertainty, so refreshing need not be forbidden — only
      made pointless. [conjecture]
38.5.1. This is a defensible content for a moral element at the
        protocol layer: it removes the occasion rather than
        demanding constant restraint against it.
38.6. Two properties come free: a batching client is largely an
      offline client, which matches intermittent connectivity;
      and local-time scheduling spreads load across longitudes
      rather than producing a global thundering herd.
38.7. The failure mode is not slowness but unpredictable
      slowness. Predictable slowness reads as rhythm; variable
      slowness reads as broken. [principle]
```

## Part VII — The client

```
39. What does forbidding arbitrary code execution in the client
    buy?
39.1. The client becomes an actual user agent — a program whose
      only principal is the user. [principle]
39.1.1. On the present web the remote party's code executes
        locally with the user's data and authority, so the local
        machine cannot be on the user's side. Every downstream
        privacy failure follows from this one arrangement.
39.2. It restores prevention for a valuable band of cases by
      providing a reference monitor the application cannot
      subvert. (cf. 8.1)
39.2.1. Capability requests are mediated by something the
        application cannot reach around.
39.2.2. Key material never enters application context.
39.2.3. Chrome is unspoofable, so phishing and dark patterns
        lose their surface.
39.3. It makes verification real rather than theatrical.
39.3.1. On the web, client-side verification is impossible in
        principle: a check performed by code the server sent is
        a server checking its own homework. [theorem]
39.3.2. A fixed client verifies signatures, checks consistency
        proofs, exchanges heads, and audits peers as background
        behavior the application cannot disable. This is what
        converts 13.1 from intention to infrastructure.
39.4. Programmability inverts: the user gains it to the degree
      the application loses it. [theorem]
39.4.1. Universal search, archiving, filtering, notification
        rules, and accessibility rendering work uniformly
        because meaning does not vary per application.
39.4.2. Arbitrary code execution is the nominalist escape hatch
        made concrete — it asserts that the kinds are whatever
        can be computed. Closing it is the practical assertion
        that they are real.
39.5. Two surfaces collapse entirely: the tracking apparatus,
      which is overwhelmingly a scripting phenomenon; and the
      exploit classes rooted in compiling adversary-supplied
      code at runtime.

40. What does it cost?
40.1. A genuine innovation ceiling: interaction models not yet
      conceived cannot be expressed. Vertical integration
      answers this for the settled majority and remains a bet on
      the remainder. [disputed]
40.2. The taxonomy becomes the bottleneck, since every new
      capability is a protocol change. This concentrates the
      price of the whole design in one place. (see 47.obj.1)
40.3. Some artifacts are irreducibly computation — games,
      simulations, creative tools — and want to be native
      applications rather than content. Decide this deliberately
      rather than discovering it and bolting on an escape hatch.
40.4. Historical pressure toward the hatch is real: HTML
      acquired scripting under advertiser demand for measurement
      and interactivity. A product sold directly to households
      has no such constituency, which is a business-model
      guarantee rather than a technical one. [conjecture]

41. Can a client verify that a server runs the code it claims?
41.1. No. Not merely difficult — impossible in the general case.
      [theorem]
41.1.1. Code on a machine its operator controls can be modified
        by that operator, and any self-measurement is another
        claim the modified server makes as easily as the honest
        one.
41.1.2. This is "never trust the client" with the roles
        reversed, and it fails for identical reasons.
41.1.3. Trust bottoms out in a compiler or a person regardless.
41.2. Trusted hardware relocates the trusted third party to a
      manufacturer rather than eliminating it, requires specific
      hardware, and has been broken repeatedly. Rejected.
41.3. Succinct proofs of execution are the only principled
      answer, and prove the computation rather than the inputs,
      and say nothing about what the server did in addition.
      Worth tracking; not worth building on presently.
41.4. The correct reframing: ask not whether the server runs the
      right code but what breaks if it does not. [principle]
41.4.1. A server that holds no truth has little to lie about, so
        code identity matters in proportion to what the code was
        trusted with.
41.4.2. Design rule: for every guarantee, determine whether it
        rests on the data structure or on the server's good
        behavior, and migrate everything possible to the former.
        The residue is the actual exposure and should be short
        and explicitly known.
41.5. Federation substitutes for attestation: redundancy across
      independently controlled parties degrades gracefully where
      an enclave collapses. [principle]
41.5.1. This is also the honest reading of what mining bought —
        not verified code, but enough independent parties that
        no single one's dishonesty decides the outcome.

## Part VIII — Sovereignty over one's data

```
42. Can a person own data about himself?
42.1. No. Property is exclusive; facts are not. Another's
      knowing my birthday does not deprive me of it.
      [principle]
42.1.1. The nominalist construal — data as an arbitrary bundle
        made property by stipulation — produced data markets and
        consent-as-alienation, and the resulting structures are
        absurd because the category was wrong.
42.2. The realist construal: a datum is a sign signifying a fact
      about a substance. That relation is not ownership and is
      not severable by agreement. [definition]
42.3. The questions that admit answers are custody, fidelity,
      fittingness, and legibility. "Control forever" is not
      among them.

43. What governs whether a use is appropriate?
43.1. Contextual integrity: the appropriate flow of information
      relative to the norms of the relationship in which it was
      shared. [definition]
43.1.1. A realist can ground this: the medical relation has a
        real form ordered to the patient's health, and a use
        ordered against him is a privation of that form — a
        defect in the thing, not a violated preference.
43.1.2. Therefore the norm attaches to the kind of relationship,
        which is the sort of thing the taxonomy already models,
        and purpose-binding in capabilities becomes mechanically
        checkable rather than free text.
43.2. Most personal data is relational, so single-owner models
      are ontologically wrong: a photograph of a child taken by
      a cousin, a message between two people, a genome
      implicating siblings. [principle]
43.2.1. Support joint standing: several subjects with real but
        different relations — author, subject, custodian,
        witness — and correspondingly different rights of
        notification, objection, correction, and
        co-authorization.

44. What is actually achievable?
44.1. Custody: the data lives in one's own store and is served
      from it. Everything else depends on this.
44.2. Origination control: the first disclosure is one's own.
      The only absolute on the list.
44.3. Legibility of access: every access is an event — who,
      when, under which capability, for what stated purpose.
      This falls out of the log at no cost and no major platform
      offers it. [observed]
44.4. Prospective revocation only, and the interface should say
      so rather than implying a control that does not exist.
44.5. Purpose attestation: misuse cannot be prevented, but a
      signed and logged statement of purpose converts misuse
      from an unfalsifiable dispute into a documented lie. This
      is 8.1 applied to consent.
44.6. Correction rights follow from fidelity: if a sign should
      signify truly, a channel to contest and correct repairs a
      defect rather than granting a courtesy.

45. What is the structural inversion?
45.1. Move the computation to the data rather than the data to
      the computation. [principle]
45.1.1. Copying everything to the computing party's servers
        forfeits control by construction; running the query
        locally and returning only the answer preserves custody,
        visibility, and the ability to revoke.
45.2. The disclosure modes form a utility-control spectrum:
      handing over a copy, query access, noised aggregates,
      approved computation returning results only, multiparty
      computation. Real designs live in the middle.

46. Should data be salable?
46.1. Distinguish two things. [principle]
46.1.1. Works one produces — writing, photographs, software,
        curriculum — are genuinely alienable, already handled by
        copyright, and licensing them is ordinary and good.
        Custody makes this better than the platform status quo.
46.1.2. Facts about oneself: markets here are a mistake. Value
        exists only in aggregate so the price signal is broken;
        the sale is permanent while payment is one-time; most
        such facts implicate others; and some goods are
        corrupted by being made fungible. [disputed]
46.2. Build the granting machinery excellently and build no
      market in facts about persons. Compensated access to works
      falls out of the same mechanism.

47. What is the realistic scope of all this?
47.1. Extraction on the present internet is a business model,
      not a missing protocol feature, and no protocol compels a
      party who does not want custody-based access to accept it.
      [observed]
47.2. But within a family, parish, school, or federation of
      small communities, the parties are known and the
      relationships durable, and sovereignty is fully achievable
      with machinery already designed: custody is the bucket,
      legibility is the log, granting is capabilities,
      revocation is crypto-shredding.
47.3. The framing to carry: not ownership of facts, which is
      incoherent, but custodianship of the record, party status
      in every disclosure, and visibility of what happens.
      [principle]
```

## Part IX — Limits and objections

```
48. What can this architecture never provide?
48.1. Liveness. Cryptography proves a server cheated and never
      makes it answer. Availability is a systems and economics
      problem throughout. [theorem]
48.2. Adequacy of the sign to the thing. Every provenance chain
      bottoms out in a human claim; a perfectly signed statement
      that a photograph is unretouched is worth what the signer
      is worth. (see 2.3, 25.1)
48.3. Meaning of a signature beyond "the holder of key K emitted
      this." Not truth, not sincerity.
48.4. Binding a key to a person, which is always an
      extra-cryptographic act — fingerprint comparison, meeting
      face to face, knowing a brother's voice.
48.4.1. Here a family or parish federation has a structural
        advantage: it possesses the physical trust graph that
        global systems had to invent expensive substitutes for.
        [observed]
48.5. Prevention surviving authorization. Once someone may read,
      he may copy and retell.
48.6. Concealment of metadata at acceptable cost. Assume the
      social graph is visible to whoever routes.
48.7. Recovery from key loss, except socially.
48.8. Choice of policy. It enforces authority structures
      faithfully and has no opinion about which are just.

49. Objections.
49.obj.1. Objection: the taxonomy cannot be gotten right in
          advance. Thirty years of settled use cases is a claim
          about the past, and a protocol that cannot be extended
          without a version bump will be wrong about the future
          in ways that matter, with no recourse.
49.obj.1.1. Reply: partial. Vertical integration and 1.0-and-done
            make the bet deliberate rather than accidental, and
            9.2.5 argues the frozen artifact is what makes
            verification hold. But no reply establishes that the
            taxonomy will be adequate, and this remains the
            largest single risk in the design. Reply slot
            deliberately left incomplete. [disputed]
49.obj.2. Objection: a single implementation is a monoculture;
          one flaw is universal, whereas ecosystem diversity
          contains failures.
49.obj.2.1. Reply: diversity distributes risk but multiplies
            unreviewed surface, and 9.1 argues that under cheap
            verification the small auditable artifact wins. The
            trade is real, and it makes deep verification
            obligatory rather than optional.
49.obj.3. Objection: mandatory attributability forecloses
          anonymous reporting of misconduct by someone with
          standing in the community — precisely the case where
          the vulnerable most need to speak.
49.obj.3.1. Reply: granted against mandatory identification,
            which is why 26.1 separates it from attributability.
            Anonymous credentials with quorum-recoverable
